resources.string: Learn Discover Canada chapter by chapter
Explore the people and events that shaped Canada
Learn your rights and duties as a Canadian citizen
Learn how elections and voting work

Canada\'s history begins with Indigenous peoples who lived on this land for thousands of years. The three distinct groups recognized today are First Nations, Inuit, and Métis, each with unique cultures, languages, and traditions.

French explorer Jacques Cartier made three voyages across the Atlantic in the 1500s, claiming land for France. In 1608, Samuel de Champlain established the first permanent European settlement at Quebec City.
The economy in New France was driven by the fur trade, fostered by French traders known as coureurs des bois and voyageurs in close partnership with Indigenous allies.
The Quebec Act allowed French Canadians religious freedom to practice Catholicism, restored French civil law, and laid early constitutional foundations for Canadian accommodation and diversity.
Canadian militia, British soldiers, and Indigenous warriors joined forces to defeat American invasions between 1812 and 1814, fostering national pride and protecting Canadian independence.
On July 1, 1867, the British North America Act created the Dominion of Canada. Sir John A. Macdonald became Canada\'s first Prime Minister, uniting Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick.
The completion of the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1885 fulfilled a national promise to connect British Columbia to eastern Canada, opening settlement across the Prairies.
Over 600,000 Canadians served in World War I. The Canadian Corps\' victory at the Battle of Vimy Ridge in April 1917 became a defining milestone of Canadian unity and international sacrifice.
In World War II, over one million Canadians served. On D-Day, June 6, 1944, the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division successfully captured Juno Beach in Normandy.
In 1982, Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau patriated the Constitution, adding the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms to permanently entrench democratic rights and human dignity.
Issued by King George III following the Seven Years\' War, it established British government in Quebec and officially recognized Indigenous land rights.
Following the American Revolution, over 40,000 Loyalists fled to Canada, expanding settlements in Nova Scotia and Quebec, leading to the creation of New Brunswick and Upper Canada.
Reformers in Upper and Lower Canada demanded democratic government. Lord Durham\'s subsequent report recommended uniting the Canadas and granting responsible self-rule.
Louis Riel led the Red River Resistance in 1869 and North-West Resistance in 1885 to defend Métis land and culture, leading directly to Manitoba joining Confederation.
Discovery of gold in Yukon in 1896 brought thousands of prospectors north, inspiring northern development and leading to Yukon\'s creation as a territory in 1898.
Suffragettes led by Nellie McClung won women\'s right to vote in 1918. The Famous Five won the 1929 Persons Case, establishing that women were legal persons under law.
The severe economic crisis of the 1930s led to creation of the Bank of Canada, unemployment insurance, and foundational federal social safety programs.
Lester B. Pearson won the 1957 Nobel Peace Prize for establishing UN Peacekeeping during the Suez Crisis. He also introduced Canada\'s iconic Maple Leaf flag in 1965.
Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau passed this milestone law making English and French official languages of the federal government and national public services.
Canada acknowledges historic wrongs, including the Residential Schools system, committing to genuine reconciliation and honoring Indigenous heritage and self-determination.
The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms forms part of Canada\'s Constitution, protecting fundamental human rights and freedoms for everyone residing in Canada.
Canadians enjoy freedom of conscience and religion, freedom of thought and expression, freedom of peaceful assembly, and freedom of association.
Every Canadian citizen aged 18 or older has the constitutional right to vote in federal, provincial, and territorial elections and to run for public office.
Canadian citizens and permanent residents have the right to move to and take up residence in any province or territory, and to seek employment anywhere in Canada.
Everyone has the right to life, liberty, and security of person, protection against unreasonable search, and habeas corpus ensuring fair and prompt legal proceedings.
All individuals are equal before and under the law without discrimination based on race, national origin, religion, sex, age, or disability. Men and women enjoy equal legal rights.
English and French are the official languages of Canada, ensuring Canadians can receive federal government services in either official language across the country.
An essential responsibility of Canadian citizenship is respecting Canada\'s laws. No individual, government official, or police officer is above the law.
Serving on a jury when called is a vital civic duty that ensures fair trials. Voting in elections keeps Canadian democracy strong and representative.
Citizens contribute to Canada by helping others in the community, volunteering, and protecting Canada\'s natural environment and cultural heritage for future generations.
The 1215 English Magna Carta laid foundational legal traditions: freedom under law, habeas corpus, and protection against arbitrary state power.
Section 35 of the Constitution Act 1982 recognizes and affirms existing treaty and land rights of First Nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples across Canada.
Canadian policy recognizes the cultural diversity of citizens as a fundamental characteristic of Canadian identity, heritage, and national strength.
Men and women have equal legal rights. Forced marriage, domestic abuse, honor crimes, and gender discrimination are strictly illegal in Canada.
Contributing time to local charities, food banks, schools, and civic groups is a cherished cornerstone of Canadian community spirit and solidarity.
Speech in Canada is free, but hate speech, incitement to violence, and defamation are illegal under Criminal Code provisions.
Citizens can own land, homes, and businesses, supported by impartial commercial laws and secure private property protections.
Serving in the Canadian Armed Forces or reservists is a honored way to defend Canadian sovereignty, security, and international humanitarian relief.
Employers and public institutions must accommodate religious practices unless doing so causes undue hardship or breaches fundamental Canadian laws.
Pledging allegiance to King Charles III, obeying Canadian laws, and fulfilling civic duties marks a proud commitment to Canada and fellow citizens.
Canada is a parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy. Our system combines elected representatives with the historical stability of the Crown.
His Majesty King Charles III is Canada\'s Sovereign and Head of State. The Governor General represents the Sovereign at the federal level across Canada.
The Prime Minister is the head of government in Canada, directing the executive branch and leading the political party with the most seats in the House of Commons.
Cabinet ministers are chosen by the Prime Minister to oversee federal government departments such as Finance, Health, Defense, and Foreign Affairs.
The House of Commons is the green chamber of Parliament, made up of Members of Parliament (MPs) directly elected by citizens in 338 electoral districts.
The Senate is the red chamber of Parliament. Senators are appointed on the Prime Minister\'s recommendation to review bills and represent regional interests.
Government is divided into executive (Prime Minister & Cabinet), legislative (Parliament: House & Senate), and judicial (independent courts) branches.
Federal handles national defense and foreign policy; provincial manages health care and education; municipal handles local services like snow removal and fire protection.
A proposed law (Bill) must pass three readings in both the House of Commons and Senate, then receive Royal Assent from the Governor General to become law.
The Supreme Court of Canada in Ottawa is the highest court in the land, consisting of nine judges led by the Chief Justice, safeguarding constitutional law.
Representatives of the Sovereign in each of Canada\'s 10 provinces, appointed by the Governor General to grant provincial Royal Assent.
Head of government in a province, leading the provincial cabinet and directing provincial policy and administration.
Appointed representatives of the federal government in Yukon, NWT, and Nunavut fulfilling ceremonial roles similar to Lieutenant Governors.
Non-partisan professional civil servants carrying out daily federal and provincial administrative operations, serving whichever party is elected.
Daily 45-minute parliamentary session where opposition MPs question Cabinet ministers about government policies and executive decisions.
An MP elected by peers to enforce parliamentary rules, maintain order, and manage House debates neutrally and impartially.
Changing Canada\'s Constitution requires approval from Parliament and at least 7 provinces representing 50% of the Canadian population.
Federal funds distributed to provinces to ensure comparable healthcare, higher education, and public services nationwide regardless of provincial wealth.
Historical gothic buildings on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, featuring the Peace Tower and iconic House of Commons and Senate chambers.
Constitutional convention requiring all Cabinet ministers to publicly support government decisions or resign from Cabinet.
Federal general elections are held at least once every four years on fixed dates, managed independently and non-partisantly by Elections Canada.
Canada is divided into 338 electoral districts or ridings. Citizens in each riding elect one Member of Parliament (MP) to represent them in Ottawa.
To vote in a federal election, you must be a Canadian citizen, at least 18 years old on election day, and registered on the National Register of Electors.
Voting in Canada is conducted by secret ballot. No one can see or force you to reveal how or for whom you cast your vote.
Voters receive a Voter Information Card detailing their polling station. Voters present valid identification proving identity and address before casting a ballot.
The party winning the most seats forms government. If they hold over 170 seats, it is a majority government; under 170 seats is a minority government.
The political party with the second-largest number of seats in the House of Commons becomes the Official Opposition, questioning and scrutinizing government policy.
Canadians can choose from several national political parties representing diverse political philosophies, or run as independent candidates.
Daily during parliamentary sittings, opposition MPs ask Cabinet ministers direct questions regarding government actions and public policies.
Voting rights expanded over time: women won federal voting rights in 1918 led by suffragettes like Nellie McClung, and First Nations gained full voting rights in 1960.
Independent, non-partisan agency responsible for organizing federal elections, maintaining voter rolls, and enforcing election finance laws.
Permanent database of eligible Canadian voters updated continuously through tax returns, provincial driver records, and citizenship updates.
Official notice mailed to registered voters before an election indicating designated polling station locations, dates, and voting hours.
Polling stations open several days prior to election day allowing citizens unable to vote on election day to cast early ballots.
Voting option by mail or at Elections Canada offices for citizens traveling, living abroad, or studying away from home.
Special elections held between general elections when an MP seat becomes vacant due to resignation or death.
Any eligible voter can run as a candidate by gathering local voter signatures and submitting nomination papers to Elections Canada.
Canada\'s electoral system where the candidate receiving the highest number of votes in a riding wins the seat.
The Governor General officially dissolves Parliament on the Prime Minister\'s advice, triggering the election campaign.
Local elections held every 3 to 4 years to elect city mayors, city councillors, and school board trustees.
Canada spans five distinct geographic regions: Atlantic Provinces, Central Canada, Prairie Provinces, West Coast, and Northern Territories.
Ottawa is the capital city of Canada. Canada consists of 10 provinces and 3 territories, stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific and north to the Arctic Ocean.
Comprising Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick. New Brunswick is Canada\'s only officially bilingual province.
Ontario and Quebec home over half of Canada\'s population. Ontario is Canada\'s industrial heartland, while Quebec is the center of French language and culture.
Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta are famous for vast agricultural plains, wheat fields, energy resources, and scenic parklands.
British Columbia is Canada\'s Pacific province, renowned for majestic Rocky Mountains, temperate rainforests, busy sea ports, and multicultural cities.
Yukon, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut cover one-third of Canada\'s landmass. Nunavut ("Our Land") was established in 1999 as a homeland for Inuit.
Canada is bordered by three oceans: Atlantic (East), Pacific (West), and Arctic (North). The St. Lawrence Seaway connects the Great Lakes to the Atlantic.
A massive geological horseshoe covering over half of Canada, rich in ancient rock, forests, lakes, and valuable minerals like nickel, gold, and copper.
Most of Canada\'s 40 million people live in urban centers within 200 kilometers of the U.S. border, forming one of the most multicultural nations on earth.
Mountain range extending through Atlantic provinces and Quebec, featuring ancient rounded peaks, river valleys, and coastal harbors.
Five Great Lakes (Ontario, Erie, Huron, Superior, Michigan) forming the largest surface freshwater system on Earth.
Majestic mountain range along the Alberta-BC border, home to famous national parks like Banff and Jasper.
Canada\'s newest territory created in 1999, whose capital Iqaluit is home to vibrant Inuit culture and Arctic wildlife.
Spectacular atmospheric light displays visible in Canada\'s northern skies caused by solar particles interacting with Earth\'s magnetic field.
Climate ranges from mild maritime on the Pacific coast to cold continental inland winters and arctic polar tundra in the far north.
Economy supported by rich natural wealth: forestry, hydroelectricity, agriculture, oil, gas, and mining for gold, diamonds, and nickel.
Over 40 national parks protecting ecological wilderness from Pacific Rim in BC to Gros Morne in Newfoundland.
Toronto (largest city), Montreal (second largest French-speaking city in the world), Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton, and Winnipeg.
Canada spans six time zones: Pacific, Mountain, Central, Eastern, Atlantic, and Newfoundland Time.
